case_study_insert.main_stem: Kestrel Bay Resort (KBR) is a private limited company in the hospitality sector, operating a 60-room seaside hotel and employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2007 by Anika Kestrel, the resort has a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KBR plans to invest $720,000 in a new sea-view wing and rooftop pool, financed by a $420,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $432,000 a year, a variable cost of $40 a unit and a selling price of $130, and produces 10,000 units a year, where each unit is an occupied room-night. KBR faces rising guest complaints about check-in delays and breakfast waste, while absenteeism has reached 9%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Guest Services and Operations Report — Q4 2024: The resort sold 2,400 room-nights at 78% occupancy. Guest complaints about check-in fell from 29 to 17 per month, but average check-in wait is still 8 minutes. Breakfast waste is 11% of covers served. An online survey of 1,150 guests gave KBR a 4.2/5 rating, and 63% said a sea-view room justified a higher price. A skills audit shows 14 of 60 staff have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the local college costs $900 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kestrel Bay Resort as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing debt-service costs for variable-rate borrowers. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.85 to $13.60 an hour, lifting payroll costs for hotels. (3) Energy and laundry input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while regional tourist arrivals grew 4.2% and guests are more price-sensitive.

questions.question_text: KBR plans to fund part of its $720,000 sea-view wing with $300,000 retained profit rather than a $420,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for KBR of using retained profit instead of the loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge or scheduled repayment, so KBR keeps its cash flow intact while it absorbs fixed costs of $432,000 a year and services the $420,000 bank loan it still needs. Every dollar not paid as loan interest can instead fund the extra housekeeping and laundry needed to cut the 11% breakfast waste and shorten the 8-minute check-in wait, helping protect the $130 selling price and the $90 contribution on each occupied room-night.

Point 2: Using $300,000 of its own money avoids the collateral and repossession risk tied to a bank loan, so the new sea-view wing cannot be seized if occupancy disappoints. It also leaves Anika Kestrel's ownership and control undisturbed: no lender can impose conditions on how the flat, democratic resort is run. This matters because 63% of the 1,150 surveyed guests already say a sea-view room justifies a higher price, so KBR can capture that premium for its own shareholders rather than for a bank.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to KBR's sea-view wing, costs and financing.

questions.question_text: KBR wants to fill the new sea-view wing and lift its 78% occupancy. Consider a regional television campaign, local radio advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should KBR choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Regional television: A regional TV campaign would build awareness of the sea-view wing quickly across the whole catchment and could justify the higher price that 63% of 1,150 surveyed guests accept. However, airtime and production are very costly for a resort with fixed costs of $432,000 a year and a $420,000 loan, and much of the audience will never book a room-night, so spend wastage would be high.

Local radio: Radio is far cheaper, targets local listeners who can realistically travel to the resort, and suits urgent messages about room availability. Its weakness is narrow reach: the 4.2% growth in regional tourist arrivals brings visitors from beyond one radio catchment, so radio alone cannot sell enough of the 10,000 room-night units to fill a $720,000 extension.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel and family lifestyle influencers can show the actual sea-view rooms and rooftop pool to exactly the guests who value them, with measurable engagement at low cost per booking. Results take time to build and depend on influencer credibility, but the 4.2/5 guest rating from 1,150 reviews gives authentic material to amplify, and the appeal extends well beyond the local radio area.

Recommendation: KBR should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by small in-resort promotions. It reaches the segment already identified in the survey, costs far less than television, travels further than local radio, and converts the 4.2/5 rating into bookings for the sea-view wing. Television is rejected as unaffordable and wasteful for a 60-employee resort, and radio is rejected as too geographically narrow to exploit the 4.2% rise in tourist arrivals.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to KBR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KBR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: KBR's absenteeism has reached 9% and guest complaints about check-in delays are rising. Explain two benefits for KBR of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its workforce of 60.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the workforce of 60 a real voice in how the new sea-view wing and check-in routines are organised, which helps meet staff social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Reception and housekeeping staff who help redesign the check-in process are more likely to attend consistently, directly reducing the 9% absenteeism rate and easing pressure on KBR's flat structure and 8-minute check-in wait.

Point 2: Consulting the people who serve guests daily produces practical ideas that improve quality, for example simpler breakfast service that cuts the 11% waste and better room-ready communication that lowers the 17 monthly complaints. Greater involvement builds commitment and reduces labour turnover, avoiding repeated $900 per employee off-the-job training costs and protecting the 10,000 room-night output needed to cover $432,000 of fixed costs while the new wing beds in. With democratic leadership the 9% absence figure should fall further, protecting the 78% occupancy needed to recover the $300,000 retained profit spent on the wing.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KBR's absenteeism, complaints, training cost and output.

questions.question_text: KBR must train 14 of 60 staff who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should KBR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at reception and in the rooms is directly relevant to KBR's own check-in system and service standards, costs no course fees, and keeps staff productive while they learn, which protects the 2,400 room-nights sold last quarter and the effort behind the fall from 29 to 17 complaints. Its drawbacks are that trainers are working staff whose own duties suffer, bad habits can be copied, and there is little formal certification, which may matter if Anika Kestrel wants to evidence quality to tour operators.

Off-the-job training: The local college option at $900 per employee gives structured, up-to-date customer-service skills and a recognised certificate. For 14 staff the stated fee is 14 × $900 = $12,600, affordable next to the $720,000 wing investment. However, it removes 14 people from a workforce of 60 during busy periods, could worsen the 8-minute check-in wait, and generic content may not match KBR's exact procedures, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: KBR should choose on-the-job training first, with short college top-ups later. It is cheaper, tailored to the resort's own service routine and avoids losing 14 staff from a workforce already stretched by 9% absenteeism. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the $12,600 fee and lost shifts would hit the 78% occupancy drive, and the new sea-view wing needs consistent on-site service standards immediately. Anika Kestrel can review the 17 monthly complaints and the 4.2/5 rating after a short pilot before deciding whether the college certificate is worth $12,600 for all 14 staff.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to KBR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of KBR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to check-in service.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KBR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $432,000 ÷ ($130 − $40) = $432,000 ÷ $90 = 4,800 units. Answer: break-even output is 4,800 room-night units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $130 − $40 = $90. Answer: contribution per unit is $90.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KBR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 4,800-unit break-even output with actual output of 10,000 room-night units, giving a margin of safety of 5,200 units, to judge whether the $720,000 sea-view wing can be filled safely.
2. Contribution per unit of $90 lets KBR test discount offers: a $10 cut to $120 would leave $80 contribution, still covering the $432,000 fixed costs if volume rose, so the 63% of surveyed guests wanting a premium can be weighed against discounting.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $432,000 and $90 contribution helps set the sales target needed to service the $420,000 bank loan before committing further spending on the rooftop pool.
4. Managers can use unit cost ($432,000 ÷ 10,000 = $43.20 plus $40 variable cost = $83.20 a unit) to track the effect of the 11% breakfast waste and the 9.5% energy and laundry cost rise, benchmarking each quarter.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 4,800 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $90 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 5,200-unit margin of safety against 10,000 units; discount and premium pricing against $432,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume for the $420,000 bank loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $83.20 to tackle waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KBR's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KBR's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.57 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.79 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.07 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $85,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $95,000 + $55,000 = $220,000. For 2024, $180,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.50 and ($180,000 − $85,000) ÷ $120,000 = $95,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.79. For 2025, $220,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.57 and ($220,000 − $70,000) ÷ $140,000 = $150,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.07.

Evaluation: Both measures moved favourably. The 2024 figure rose to 1.57 in 2025, so short-term assets cover more of the $140,000 due within a year, helped by cash rising from $35,000 to $55,000. The second measure is more informative here: it climbed from 0.79 to 1.07, so KBR is no longer dependent on selling its $70,000 of inventories to pay current bills. That is reassuring while the resort services a $420,000 bank loan and funds the $720,000 sea-view wing. The concern is trade receivables, up from $60,000 to $95,000, which tie up cash; if corporate guests pay slowly the improvement could reverse, and the smaller inventory balance needs monitoring against 78% occupancy demand.

Conclusion: KBR's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose, and crucially the improvement does not rely on stock, so short-term solvency is stronger. The main residual risk is rising receivables, so tighter credit control should accompany the expansion. Weekly monitoring of the $95,000 balance would make the improvement sustainable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: KBR is considering a food-waste reduction programme to tackle the 11% breakfast waste. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KBR of this initiative.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Cutting the 11% breakfast waste lowers the food element of the $40 variable cost per room-night, widening the $90 contribution KBR earns on each of its 10,000 units and protecting profit while energy and laundry input costs have risen 9.5%. It also supports the 4.2/5 rating given by 1,150 guests: consistent breakfast quality and less waste help sustain the 63% of surveyed guests who accept a premium for a sea-view stay, strengthening the case for the $720,000 wing.

Disadvantage: Introducing portion control, better stock systems and staff training takes management time and may require small-scale equipment, which adds to the $432,000 fixed costs at a time when a $420,000 loan is being repaid. If stricter portions reduce perceived value, the 17 monthly complaints could rise again and the 4.2/5 rating might slip, offsetting the saving. The insert gives no figure for the cost of the programme or the saving from 11% waste, so the net benefit cannot be quantified and remains a judgement.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KBR's waste figure, guest rating, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in energy and laundry input costs will affect KBR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If KBR's $420,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point costs 0.75% × $420,000 = $3,150 a year (0.0075 × $420,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $432,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct interest effect is nil. The higher rate could also make future borrowing for the $720,000 wing dearer and make guests slightly more cautious about discretionary stays.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.60 an hour): KBR employs a workforce of 60 in largely hourly-paid housekeeping and service roles, so this lifts the wage bill and is not optional. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no annual total can be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 10,000 units ÷ 60 staff = about 166.7 room-nights per worker, so a higher wage is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $90 contribution shrinks. Democratic leadership and on-the-job training can help protect that productivity.

Energy and laundry input costs (9.5%): These feed the $40 variable cost on every occupied room-night. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $40 were exposed, the rise would add 9.5% × $40 = $3.80 a unit, or about $38,000 a year at 10,000 units (10,000 × $3.80). Even a smaller exposed share still reduces the $90 contribution on each room-night, and this recurs on every unit rather than once.

Conclusion: The 9.5% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 10,000 room-nights and directly erodes the $90 contribution that justifies the $720,000 extension, whereas the interest rise costs only $3,150 a year on the stated loan and the wage effect, though unavoidable, can be offset by maintaining 166.7 room-nights per worker. KBR should fix the loan rate and recover part of the input rise through the premium 63% of guests accept.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KBR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KBR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
